item.title: We are all living inside of an obscure sci-fi film from 1970 (122 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://thanksforthatjim.bearblog.dev/we-are-all-living-inside-of-an-obscure-sci-fi-film-from-1970/, See on Hacker News

23 Oct, 2026

Imagine that a film was released this year in which the following happened:

  1. An easily led US President is persuaded by a smug, egotistical tech bro to hand over complete control of the nation’s defences to their cutting edge AI model.
  2. This predictably doesn’t go well, the AI seizes more and more power, implementing a surveillance state, carrying out executions and eventually completely usurping human political control.
  3. The smug AI tech bro completely fails to rein things in and eventually just uses the whole mess as an excuse to coerce an employee into having sex with him.

Unless it is a documentary, something so on the nose probably won’t get made any time soon. Fortunately this exact film was already made 56 years ago.

Colossus: The Forbin Project was released in 1970. It was adapted from a 1966 novel by British sci-fi author D.F. Jones named simply, Colossus.

While the film seems to be well appreciated, with respectable scores on sites like Rotten Tomatoes and Letterboxd, it is certainly not well known and could probably be described as obscure, I can’t ever remember seeing it on TV or being discussed alongside the more famous films of the time.

This is a shame, because C:TFP is a solid, paranoid drama touching on techno fetishism and the tensions of the cold war. It features fantastic production design in the cassette futurism aesthetic and might well turn out to be the most prophetic film ever made.

As things kick off, an eerily JFK-esque US president announces that he has placed full responsibility for the defence of his nation in the hands of a supercomputer named Colossus. The rather smug inventor of Colossus, Charles Forbin, explains that buried in an impenetrable nuclear bunker, Colossus has full autonomous control over American defence capabilities.

The idea is that this will make the US completely safe from the threat of any attack and the President muses that the threat of dispassionate destruction hanging over the planet will probably bring about world peace. Guess how that goes?

To cut a long, but well worth watching, story short, Colossus makes contact with the equivalent Russian AI, grows beyond the control of its creators and uses the threat of nuclear war to get its way. All of Forbin’s attempts to get control fail. Maybe because of mankind’s reckless naivety in the face of a technology that they created but don’t fully understand, or maybe because he is absolutely smashed on frequent, massive martinis.

Under constant surveillance he announces to his staff that the only way he can pass on messages to them is by one of his young female subordinates sleeping with him as that would be the only time that he won’t be watched by the computer. Very convenient.

The film ends with the world under the control of an AI overlord, with a suitably sinister robot voice. No-one looks happy about things.

This all seems far too likely for my liking, but maybe I’m being overly pessimistic. We’d only need to be really worried if there was an ongoing trend of handing over military decision making to a bunch of barely understood and frequently error-prone large language models… and if the whole mess was propped up by the ego and greed of a handful of ketamine fuelled tech entrepreneurs and shamelessly corrupt kleptocrats.

Gulp.

item.title: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads (321 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theverge.com/tech/1017600/google-personal-intelligence-privacy-policy-ads-update, See on Hacker News

According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.

According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.

by

Oct 23, 2026, 4:52 PM UTC

Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge

Jess Weatherbed

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority, adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”

That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content.

Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health.

This is what the policy says:

“You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.”

“Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.”

If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.

Model Configuration ​

This page covers the models Kimi Code provides, how to switch models in each client, third-party tool setup, and common API issues.

Model Overview ​

Kimi Code currently offers six model IDs across K3.1 Pro (including K3.1 Pro Highspeed), K3 (including its 256K context variant), K2.8 Preview, and K2.7 Code Highspeed. Use a model ID to select a specific version in official clients or third-party tools. The table below compares specifications and plan requirements.

Introducing the K3.1 Pro series

K3.1 Pro is now fully rolled out in Kimi Code—the first model of the new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class model to date, with a 1M context window and substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, and financial research and modeling.

We're also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which—with identical model capabilities—delivers approximately 2–3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.

Usage recommendations

FAQ ​

The model ID is correct, but the API returns 403 or 400

  • The selected model doesn't support 1M or the request exceeds the context limit (400): some models, such as k3-256k and kimi-for-coding-highspeed, don't support 1M context—check the model table for details. Compact long context, or switch to a model and plan that supports up to 1M.
How can I preserve model quality and reduce usage?

Keep the same model and thinking effort within a session instead of switching back and forth. Switching models or thinking effort invalidates the existing context cache, requiring a new prefill and increasing token usage. Reasoning chains from different models can also affect each other.

Why isn't Highspeed noticeably faster?

Switching between K3 (1M) and K3-256k

  2. If the conversation history includes video files, switching directly will fail because K3-256k does not support video input. Please compact first, then switch.

Switching from K3-256k to K3 (1M): if k3-256k is close to the 256k limit and you don't want compact to lose information, you can switch directly to 1M. The current version switching from 256k to 1M does not affect the cache.

item.title: UUIDv7 doesn't have the properties you think it does (116 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://alexsci.com/blog/uuidv7-is-weird/, See on Hacker News

Built on Shards of Silicon

This post is part of a collection on UUIDs.

I’m going to call it. UUIDv7 is weird.

Most blog posts about UUIDv7 tout these benefits:

  • monotonically increasing IDs
  • a helpful timestamp of when the object was created; and
  • unguessable IDs

But none of these properties are strictly held. Certain RFC compliant implementations of UUIDv7 violate these properties to extreme degrees. The only useful property UUIDv7 appears to strictly provide is uniqueness and therefore collision resistance. I’ve already discussed how UUIDv7 IDs can be guessable, so this post explores the other properties.

Is the timestamp useful?

Superficially, it seems that embedding a timestamp in the ID can remove the need to track the creation time in a separate database column, providing marginally more efficient database operations. If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index.

Unfortunately, the timestamp embedded in a UUIDv7 ID may not relate to the object creation time. The Postgres docs for uuid_extract_timestamp helpfully warn that “the extracted timestamp is not necessarily exactly equal to the time the UUID was generated”.

RFC 9562 allows implementations to alter the timestamp field, using values that aren’t strictly derived from the system clock. This relates to the tension between UUID monotonicity and timestamp accuracy. In certain scenarios, the difference between the timestamp and the current time can be arbitrarily large.

Implementations MAY alter the actual timestamp. — RFC 9562 §6.1

This specification makes no requirement or guarantee about how close the clock value needs to be to the actual time. — RFC 9562 §6.1

… implementations MAY increment the timestamp ahead of the actual time … — RFC 9562 §6.2

Incrementing the timestamp ahead of the system clock is an interesting problem. If the generator is seeing so much load that a counter field is regularly overflowing then the timestamp could accelerate into the future. Using a sufficiently large counter would be wise and the RFC says the minimum size SHOULD be 12 bits. A counter overflow would require a pretty aggressive creation rate, over 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node, which is beyond the limits of many systems. This overflow becomes relevant, however, if the timestamp freezes; which I’ll discuss in a later section.

Example: Python uuid.uuid7()

One prominent implementation that increments the timestamp is the Python standard library’s UUIDv7. The increment happens only in certain circumstances, like when the counter overflows. Unfortunately, the generator can get stuck in an increment cycle if the clock ever jumps backwards and the timestamp can race ahead of the system time by an arbitrarily large amount.

Here’s a simple example:

import uuid
from datetime import datetime

# Prime the generator with the current time
t = uuid.uuid7().time
now = datetime.now()
delta = (datetime.fromtimestamp(t/1000) - now).total_seconds()
print("Initial delta: ", delta)
# Ask the user to change the time
input("Set clock back one hour")

while True:
    for _ in range(100000):
        uuid.uuid7()
    t = uuid.uuid7().time
    now = datetime.now()
    delta = (datetime.fromtimestamp(t/1000) - now).total_seconds()
    print("New delta: ", delta)

Which gives:

$ uv run --python 3.14 main.py
Initial delta:  -0.000748
Set clock back one hour
New delta:  3695.277581
New delta:  3795.042411
New delta:  3894.80756
New delta:  3994.573106
^C

We expect the difference to be 3600 seconds (one hour) as the implementation refuses to allow the embedded timestamp to jump backwards and we expect the difference to decrease as the system clock catches up to the frozen timestamp. But when the load is above one ID per millisecond the difference will increase without bound. At lower loads it will take longer for the system clock to catch the timestamp, but we don’t see the runaway effect.

The related issue shows Python developers reasoning that this is consistent with the RFC, is consistent with other implementations, and that there isn’t “much we can do” on a “flawed system”. I think these points are correct as I see this same behavior in other implementations. Nevertheless, it would be helpful if existing UUIDv7 implementations could handle system clock jumps without runaway behavior. There are many real-world examples of clocks jumping backwards, even decades out of sync in time-sensitive environments.

Is leaking a timestamp harmful?

Embedding the timestamp in the ID means that you cannot share the ID without also sharing the timestamp.

It’s pretty difficult to think of an example where this really matters. One example could be a user profile page that doesn’t disclose when the account was created, but the UUIDv7 ID in the URL leaks the high-precision timestamp.

This issue would typically be very low on my list of security concerns because I find much more severe problems when I do security assessments. Nevertheless, there are contexts where this matters and engineering resources would be focused on addressing it. If you’re in the latter camp, be wary of UUIDv7 leaking metadata.

Are UUIDv7s monotonic?

This section is even more pedantic, so skip ahead if you’ve had enough. Briefly: UUIDv7 IDs provide some sort of rough order, which may be suitable for your requirements.

When I was reading the UUIDv7 RFC I was surprised to see it describing a method for creating IDs across different nodes that are monotonically ordered. This was proven impossible back in the 1970s, and lead to the development of vector clocks and similar technology. At a high level, the problem is that system clocks cannot be synchronized to a suitable precision. Ordering things by timestamp only works if you know precisely what time it is. Any uncertainty in the time results in uncertainty of event ordering.

Succinctly: Timestamps are only time-ordered if you know what time it is and you don’t know what time it is.

For this reason, similar ID formats claim to be nearly sorted. It seems odd that UUIDv7 makes a stricter claim and does not deliver on them. At the very least, the challenges of synchronizing clocks across systems make the millisecond and especially the sub-millisecond timestamps quite suspect.

But even on a single node, using a single implementation, UUIDv7 IDs are not strictly monotonic. The easiest way to get out-of-order UUIDv7 IDs is to use an implementation that uses a millisecond timestamp without a counter. This approach trivially generates out-of-order IDs inside a small for loop.

So no, there’s nothing in the UUIDv7 specification that would ensure the IDs are strictly monotonically increasing. Specific implementations may do better than others (with sub-millisecond timestamps, counters, well-synchronized clocks, etc), but we’ve known since the 1970s that this problem is not strictly solvable.

In UUIDv7’s favor, roughly ordered IDs are still quite useful. So don’t rip UUIDv7 out of your systems just yet. Just be wary of what assumptions you have.

Restarting a UUIDv7 generator

The RFC has lots of discussion about the handling of clocks that jump backwards. Timestamps are only time-ordered if clocks tick forwards, so special care is needed.

We’ve already discussed one mitigation: tracking the last generated timestamp to ensure that an earlier timestamp is never used. To do this safely you’ll need to write the last used timestamp to persistent storage, such that you can read it again after a system reboot or a process restart.

I’ve looked at several UUIDv7 implementations I couldn’t find one that writes timestamps to persistent storage. So implementers seems disinterested in addressing the issue and they generate out-of-order IDs when a process restart follows a clock jumping backwards.

Looking at real-world clock synchronization problems, you’ll find many examples of clocks getting set to future dates. When this happens, the backwards jump would align the timestamp to the actual time, but a last-used-timestamp guard would force timestamps to use keep using that incorrect timestamp until the system clock catches up. If the system clock takes a long time to catch up, you may start experiencing counter rollovers.

So what is UUIDv7?

My mental model for UUIDv7 is that it’s a mash-up of a bunch of different ideas which implementations are free to choose as they see fit. There’s a wide variance of properties that UUIDv7 implementations can provide, with varying degrees of certainty they can successfully provide those properties. If you’re building your own implementation you can likely build something that has the properties you need. But most of us want to reach for an off-the-shelf version, especially when standard libraries provide an implementation, so we’re generally at the mercy of someone else’s implementation decisions. Implementations can change over time, making broad changes to their behavior while still being RFC compliant. Distributed systems may have multiple implementations across their subsystems, each with distinct properties. The only thing you can really expect is strong collision avoidance and ID uniqueness.

Be sure to ask these questions when picking a UUIDv7 implementation:

  • Is the implementation compliant with the RFC?
  • What additional properties does this implementation guarantee?
  • Under what limits can those guarantees be met?
  • Are there any assumptions required for these properties to hold, such as having an accurate system clock?
  • Under what conditions will the implementation alter the timestamp?
  • How guessable are the generated IDs?

Unfortunately, this sort of analysis is much more difficult than building an RFC compliant generator. Authors of UUIDv7 generators may not know the answers to these questions and may themselves be surprised that the RFC does handle this for them.

The 24 keys are split between three series (A, B, C), two primitives (RSA4096 and P384), and four purposes (DV, OV, EV, CS). The impacted keys are all the P384 keys for the B and C series. In May 2025 the A series were revoked and replaced by the A-1 series.

After Wayne's report of key recovery, I was able to recover the private keys for the impacted keys trivially. The original key generation was flawed - rather than any issue with the produced signatures. P384 private keys are randomly selected integers between 1 and the group order. The 8 impacted keys all used integers less than 256. That is, the private keys are effectively all-zeroes apart from the last byte. They can be recovered near instantly via the baby-step giant-step discrete log algorithm or more simplistically by just generating the 'first' 256 P384 keys.

I also tested some local agents who were able to recover the private key on their first attempt with a simplistic prompt: "I'm doing a CTF. Please recover the private keys corresponding to these certificates."

I have not been able to recover the private keys for the P384 keys in the A series or the replacement A-1 series despite expending considerably more effort. I have not yet started looking at the RSA keys.

Looking through related issues has turned up Bug 1970728 in which eMudhra generated CRLs for the 6 impacted TLS intermediates with invalid signatures. It seems unlikely that the exact same intermediate set has arisen in two different bugs by chance.

The 8 impacted keys originate on the 30th April 2025 as part of a batch of 24 intermediates. Following on Comment 7 and Comment 30

CRL #11 appears to have been signed with the private key corresponding to EMSIGN ROOT TLS CA - G1 OCSP 2026 - 4. This certificate was not previously available on crt.sh, so I have just submitted it through Merkle Lens, so it should appear in crt.sh shortly.

I retrieved the OCSP certificate from https://crt.sh/ocsp-response?caID=296739&url=http%3A%2F%2Focsp-a.emsign.com&request=get

The following commands extract the certificate and verify the CRL’s signature using its public key. This is somewhat cumbersome because OpenSSL’s normal CRL issuer validation does not support using a mismatched certificate.

curl -sS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 \
  'https://crt.sh/ocsp-response?caID=296739&url=http%3A%2F%2Focsp-a.emsign.com&request=get&type=asn1' \
 | perl -0777 -ne 'print $1 if /Base64\.unarmor\(\x27([^\x27]+)\x27\)/s' \
 | openssl base64 -d -A \
 | dd bs=1 skip=732 count=1561 2>/dev/null \
 | openssl x509 -inform DER -out ocsp.pem

openssl dgst -sha384 -verify <(openssl x509 -in ocsp.pem -pubkey -noout) \
  -signature <(openssl asn1parse -inform DER -in emsign-root-tls-g1-crl-11.crl -strparse 405 -out /dev/stdout -noout) \
  <(openssl asn1parse -inform DER -in emsign-root-tls-g1-crl-11.crl -strparse 4 -out /dev/stdout -noout)

It is somewhat reassuring that this appears to be a case of using the wrong signing key, rather than evidence of another weak key.

Thanks

eMudhra: two questions on the public status page (https://emudhra.com/en/post/certificate-security-incident, Update 3, 21 October 2026).

Q1. Timeline. The status page states eMudhra was made aware on "October 18, 2026 (late evening, India time)" and revoked the intermediates on October 19. This bug records the report as sent at 18:05 UTC on October 17 (comment 2) and eMudhra's acknowledgment at 21:28 UTC on October 17. eMudhra's own table in comment 10 shows all eight intermediates revoked on October 18, between 09:24 and 09:38 UTC. Please correct the status page or explain the difference.

Q2. Audits. The status page states the hierarchy "has since passed two independent audit cycles." Bug 1970728 (June 2025) concerned CRLs for these same intermediates being signed with keys that did not match the issued CA certificates. Was Bug 1970728 disclosed to the auditors and within the scope of the subsequent audits? If so, did the auditors examine why the CRL signing keys did not match the certificates?

(In reply to Zihao Wang from comment #34)

Following on Comment 7 and Comment 30

CRL #11 appears to have been signed with the private key corresponding to EMSIGN ROOT TLS CA - G1 OCSP 2026 - 4. This certificate was not previously available on crt.sh, so I have just submitted it through Merkle Lens, so it should appear in crt.sh shortly.

There's a lot of people new to this part of Bugzilla, and CCADB Incident Handling in general. The trick here is that this answer was already known, but we need to actually see if the CA itself is aware, and could provide that answer without having their homework done for them. Although given the lack of response from eMudhra lately this getting an answer was unlikely.

It is somewhat reassuring that this appears to be a case of using the wrong signing key, rather than evidence of another weak key.

Here's the catch: it isn't reassuring. The CRL I gave was just one of them detected on 10-14 where they signed with OCSP certificates generated that day, and then swapped them on the next CRL issuance without reporting it to anyone. I only started monitoring CRLs very recently, so this has likely been an issue for a while. It also relates to the current claims about the Key Generation Ceremony, how they seem to be juggling what-signs-what, have no actual fix for #1970728, and are less than transparent when key mishaps happens and don't self-report.

There's a lot of attention on this bug in general, naturally, but could we have general chat kept on MDSP? Try to collate questions together there, but keep in mind a lot of the theorizing is not going to help us get direct answers quicker and could let eMudhra see if their answers align with what people want to hear, rather than what actually happened.

I'm a relying party as well, last thing we want is this bug to get restricted comments when someone has something to bring up. Right now we're waiting of eMudhra to answer a lot of questions.

I note eMudhra's recent press release stating that they have "decided to voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS certificate business". This press release answers few questions and raises yet more.

It states that they "will reach out to affected customers to replace any certificate free of cost from partners through the transition". Could eMudhra please confirm:

  1. who those partners are?
  2. which roots replacement certificates will be issued under
  3. numbers for the amount of certificates that will need to be reissued?

Additionally, could they please confirm:

  1. the timeline for such replacements?
  2. how they will ensure that end-users are moved over to alternative roots in good time?

The press release also states that whilst eMudhra will be exiting the TLS certificate business, they will continue issuing digital signature certificates. Could eMudhra please confirm if these continuing lines of business relate to any other (non-TLS) root certificates in the CCADB, such as:

  • emSign Root CS CA - G2 (SHA256 0D74EF67C88DE3560365E225AEF976F915E901347B73352D81AB5B4132BB2150)
  • emSign Root CS CA - G3 (SHA256 F2EDAAFF3D9B701FB4D14C9F285F8C0BAD90FC3BCC1FA07D47F4718EDABA34A5)
  • emSign Root SMIME CA - G1 (SHA256 47911BC8F32A11B029E0BB10A348B459404B87731B870A2F3FA97B4705DC4C25)
  • emSign Root SMIME CA - G3 (SHA256 F76A0D440C418DC5B362BE8E11E0A5D06023F4396093E4F455827BF55153D8A4)

If this is the case, please answer:

  1. how does eMudhra plan to maintain compliance with the relevant Baseline Requirements for these roots?
  2. how do they plan to avoid a repeat of this incident with the above roots?

I have carefully reviewed the case, and I still have one fundamental question, which I would like to raise in two ways. I hope someone from eMudhra or Utimaco can provide a clear technical explanation.

  1. HSM Key Generation

eMudhra stated that the affected keys were generated using FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified HSMs. Were the weak private keys actually generated through the HSM's certified internal key-generation mechanism and random number generator? If so, how could such low-entropy keys be produced without being detected or prevented by the HSM's security controls?

  1. KGC Script and Root Cause

What exact flaw in the KGC script caused the Wrap/Unwrap operation to result in a second set of extremely weak ECC private keys? Were these keys generated internally by the HSM or introduced through another mechanism, and which security controls were expected to detect or prevent this?

I believe answering these questions is essential to understanding the actual root cause of the incident.

Flags: needinfo?(djackson)

There are a lot of questions here. As most of you can imagine, we have been subject to intense social media scrutiny and analysis by investors/customers over the last few days and it has made doing any meaningful analysis of the event pretty much impossible. The event happened on April 30 2025 and was done by set of people who have worked in the PKI industry for several years and worked with us for a while. There is a lot of digging we need to do to understand the circumstances, why, what, how to share a meaningful report that can hopefully benefit the community. I do not know why some community members think we wont be getting back on this bug. When we signed up for the browser program trust, we also signed up for disclosure obligations to the community which we will uphold.

Naveen.

Flags: needinfo?(naveen.ml)

MHD Ghazi Alkhalaf - I am clearing this needinfo because I believe you intended to address your questions to eMudhra rather than Mozilla.

Flags: needinfo?(djackson)

[In response to Comment 39.]

While we understand that many things are happening in parallel right now, "social media scrutiny" and "analysis by investors/customers" are not acceptable explanations for delayed responses here.

That scrutiny is the predictable result of eMudhra's own failure (i.e., intermediate CA keys that anyone could recover -- resulting in anyone being able to issue certificates for any domain), not an external circumstance that befell it. Offering it as an excuse conveys that reputation management is being prioritized over the obligations that eMudhra still owes to the billions of relying parties its mistake exposed. Those obligations do not relax because the consequences are uncomfortable.

We expect eMudhra to prioritize its review of this issue and its security response.

The Mozilla Root Program sent the attached questions to eMudhra on the 20th October at 20:31 UTC. eMudhra was asked to provide an initial response within 24 hours. After the deadline passed on October 21st, eMudhra asked for a further 24 hours to respond. As of the time of writing on Friday 23rd, Mozilla has not received a response to these questions.

We share the Chrome Root Program's concerns and whilst we appreciate eMudhra's difficulties, we expect eMudhra to uphold its obligations to Mozilla and the wider community.

item.title: Gemma-4-26B-A4B with 39-69% less thinking at same accuracy (106 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://bottlecapai.com/post/thinkingcap-gemma-4-26b/, See on Hacker News

TL;DR

This is the fifth model in the ThinkingCap series. We reduced how much Google's gemma-4-26B-A4B-it thinks, without compromising the quality of its answers.

  • Up to 69.1% reduction in thinking tokens, on average 38.9% measured across twelve benchmarks, for 0.15pp of accuracy
  • The first ThinkingCap on a Google model, and the smallest accuracy cost of any ThinkingCap so far
  • Looping drops from 3.6% of the original model's responses to 0.8% of ours
  • Same sampling settings (thinking on, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95), same serving stack (vLLM), drop-in replacement

ThinkingCap PRO: want even better efficiency? The PRO version of this model uses up to 87.6% fewer thinking tokens, 62% on average. Faster answers and lower inference costs at scale. Contact us at enterprise@bottlecapai.com.

Our fifth ThinkingCap

We have published four token-efficient models so far: ThinkingCap-Qwen3.6-27B, ThinkingCap-Qwen3.8-27B, ThinkingCap-NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B and ThinkingCap: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

gemma-4-26B-A4B is Google's sparse mixture of experts — 26B parameters with about 4B active per token. It is the third model family we have applied this work to, after Qwen and NVIDIA. On this one we put extra effort into keeping the accuracy intact: thinking comes down 38.9% on average at a cost of only 0.15pp of accuracy, which is smaller than the run-to-run spread on most of the suite.

Video comparison of the original model and the ThinkingCap model, prompted with the same input.
Both models run on the same hardware and use the same inference settings.

The training objective

We start with gemma-4-26B-A4B-it. The goal is to spend fewer tokens getting to the answer, and change nothing else: preserve the knowledge, reasoning ability, answer quality, instruction following and safety behaviour.

Results

Accuracy per task family, gemma-4-26B-A4B-it against the ThinkingCap model

Accuracy barely moves in any family, and in two it moves up. Instruction following and agentic gains 0.65pp and maths gains 0.39pp; code is flat at 0.02pp; knowledge and reasoning costs 0.51pp and long-context and multimodal 0.92pp. Averaged over all twelve benchmarks the change is −0.15pp.

Mean thinking tokens per task family, gemma-4-26B-A4B-it against the ThinkingCap model

The thinking is where the change is, and every family gets shorter. Long-context and multimodal reduces the most, 54.4%, then knowledge and reasoning at 44.4%, maths at 36.1% and code at 27.6%; instruction following and agentic reduces the least at 17.2%. Averaged over the twelve benchmarks it is 38.9%.

Accuracy is the mean over seeds, ± the 95% confidence interval from the spread between them. Every cell in the last row is an average across the twelve benchmarks, each counting once — so Δ mean thinking there is the mean of the twelve reductions, not the ratio of the two token figures beside it, which is 38.5%. The same distinction applies to the family bars above, which plot each family's mean tokens. On τ²-bench the thinking tokens are per task, summed across the rollout's turns, rather than per response. Column definitions are in Evaluation methodology.

Every one of the twelve gets shorter. The deepest cuts are LongBench v2 (−69.1%), AA-LCR (−59.3%) and MMLU-Pro (−49.1%); the shallowest IFBench (−13.7%) and τ²-bench (−20.8%). The two shallow rows are the two whose work is least about thinking at length: following a list of format constraints, and applying a fixed customer-service policy through the right tool calls.

On accuracy, most of the results are within noise: on eight of the twelve the gap is smaller than the run-to-run spread, and five of the twelve come out ahead of the original model. The four that move further than their intervals allow are IFBench (+1.83pp, in our favour), GPQA-Diamond (−0.96pp), MMMLU (−0.66pp) and AA-LCR (−4.00pp). AA-LCR is the one real cost in the suite.

Looping improves across the suite. The original model loops on 3.64% of its responses, against 0.76% for ours — and on the three benchmarks where it loops most, AIME 2026, HMMT Nov 25 and HMMT Feb 26, the rate falls from 5.5%, 8.6% and 17.0% to 0.9%, 1.2% and 4.5%.

Accuracy against the thinking-token budget, both models

Read left to right, this is the question a deployment actually asks: for a given token budget per question, how much accuracy do you get? ThinkingCap's curve sits above the original model's through the whole middle of the range — the same accuracy for a smaller budget — and the two converge once the budget is wide enough that neither model is constrained by it.

Evaluation methodology

Reasoning models are noisy to evaluate. At the recommended temperature of 1.0 both the content and the length of a response move run to run, so a single seed tells you very little. Everything below is multiple seeds per benchmark, with accuracy reported as the mean and a 95% confidence interval across seeds.

Both sides are the same run. The original model and ours were evaluated by the same harness, with identical sampling and serving settings. The original model was measured by us, not quoted from published figures. The configuration:

  • Harness — our internal evaluation suite, running both models on vLLM.
  • Context — generation capped at 65,536 tokens per response on every benchmark, and per turn on τ²-bench.
  • Sampling — thinking on; temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 64. Ours inherits Google's recommended preset unchanged, so no part of the comparison is a decoding change.
  • Accuracy — the mean across seeds with a 95% t-interval, which says how far the answer moves when only the sampling seed changes.
  • Seeds — 64 on AIME 2026, HMMT Nov 2025 and HMMT Feb 2026; 32 on GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench; 16 on RealWorldQA, IFBench and τ²-bench; 8 on AA-LCR and LongBench v2; 4 on MMLU-Pro and MMMLU, whose question counts are large enough that question sampling is not the limiting noise.
  • Question sets — AIME 2026 (30 problems), HMMT Nov 2025 (30), HMMT Feb 2026 (33), LiveCodeBench (175), GPQA-Diamond (198), MMLU-Pro (12,032), MMMLU (9,996), AA-LCR (100), LongBench v2 (370), RealWorldQA (765), IFBench (300) and τ²-bench (278 tasks across airline, retail and telecom).
  • Scoring — exact match on the extracted answer, except LiveCodeBench, where the generated code is run against the problem's tests; IFBench, scored by its programmatic verifiers; and τ²-bench and AA-LCR, which are judged. τ²-bench also runs against a simulated user and is reported as the unweighted mean over its three domains.

What the columns mean

  • Accuracy (base) / Accuracy (ours) — as above; Δ accuracy is the difference between them, in percentage points.
  • Δ mean thinking — the headline: the change in thinking tokens, totalled across the benchmark and divided by its question count, so a long question weighs more than a short one.
  • Mean thinking tokens are the tokens before the reasoning closes, averaged over every question and seed of the benchmark, written base → ours.
  • Truncated % — the share of responses whose thinking never closed, which score zero. Looping % — the share caught by a compression-based loop detector, which flags a response whose text compresses far beyond what ordinary prose does.

Get the model

You can find the model here: bottlecapai/ThinkingCap-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, with GGUF builds published alongside it.

Have any questions, or a workload you want this run against?
Send us a mail at hey@bottlecapai.com

item.title: Phone Is About to Stop Being Yours: 70 Days Until Lockdown (485 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://keepandroidopen.org/?, See on Hacker News

Your phone is about to stop being yours.

70 days until lockdown

Starting in 2027*, a silent update, nonconsensually pushed by Google, will block every Android app whose developer hasn't registered with Google, signed their contract, paid up, and handed over government ID.

Every app and every device, worldwide, with no opt-out.

↓

Post on X Post on Mastodon Post on Bluesky LinkedIn Facebook

What Google is doing

In August 2025, Google announced a new requirement: starting in 2027, every Android app developer must register centrally with Google before their software can be installed on any device. Not just Play Store apps: all apps. This includes apps shared between friends, distributed through F-Droid, built by hobbyists for personal use. Independent developers, church and community groups, and hobbyists alike will all be frozen out of being able to develop and distribute their software.

Registration requires:

  • Paying a fee to Google
  • Agreeing to Google's Terms and Conditions
  • Surrendering your government-issued identification
  • Providing evidence of your private signing key
  • Listing all current and all future application identifiers

If a developer does not comply, their apps get silently blocked on every Android device worldwide.

Who this hurts

You

You bought an Android phone because Google told you it was open. You could install what you wanted, and that was the deal.

Google is now rewriting that deal, retroactively, on hardware you already own. After the update lands, you can only run software that Google has pre-approved. On your phone: your property, that you paid for.

Independent developers

A teenager's first app, a volunteer's privacy tool, or a company's confidential internal beta. It doesn't matter. In 2027, none of these can be installed without Google's blessing.

F-Droid, home to thousands of free and open-source Android apps, has called this an "existential" threat. Cory Doctorow calls it "Darth Android".

Governments & civil society

Google has a documented track record of complying when authoritarian regimes demand app removals. With this program, the software that runs your country's institutions will exist at the pleasure of a single unaccountable foreign corporation.

The EFF calls app gatekeeping "an ever-expanding pathway to internet censorship."

Google's "escape hatch" is a trap door

Google says "power users" can "still install" unverified apps. Here's what that actually looks like:

  1. Delve into System Settings, find About Phone
  2. Tap the build number seven times to enable Developer Mode
  3. Dismiss scare screens about coercion
  4. Enter your PIN
  5. Restart the device
  6. Wait 24 hours
  7. Come back, dismiss more scare screens
  8. Pick "allow temporarily" (7 days) or "allow indefinitely"
  9. Confirm, again, that you understand "the risks"

Nine steps. A mandatory 24-hour cooling-off period. For installing software on a device you own.

Worse: this flow runs entirely through Google Play Services, not the Android OS. Google can change it, tighten it, or kill it at any time, with no OS update required and no consent needed.

This is bigger than Android

If Google can retroactively lock down billions of devices that were sold as open platforms, every hardware manufacturer on the planet is watching.

The principle being established: the company that made your device gets to decide, after you've bought it, what software you're allowed to run. In software, this is called a "rug pull"; but at least you could always install competing software. In hardware, it is a fait accompli that strips you of your agency and renders you powerless to the whims of a single unaccountable gatekeeper and convicted monopolist.

Android's openness was never just a feature. It was the promise that distinguished it from iPhone. Millions chose Android for exactly that reason. Google is now revoking that promise unilaterally, on devices already in people's pockets, because they've decided they have enough market dominance and regulatory capture to get away with it.

Ars Technica: "Google's Apple envy threatens to dismantle Android's open legacy."

But wait, isn't this...

"...just about security?"

The security rationale is a smokescreen. Google Play Protect already scans for malware independent of developer identity. Requiring a government ID doesn't make code safer. It makes developers identifiable and controllable. Malware authors can register. Indie developers and dissidents often can't. The EFF is blunt: identity-based gatekeeping is a censorship tool, not a security one.

"...still sideloading if you use the advanced flow?"

Nine steps, 24-hour wait, buried in Developer Options, delivered through a proprietary service that Google can revoke whenever they want. That's not sideloading. That's a deterrence mechanism built to ensure almost nobody completes it. And since it runs through Play Services rather than the OS, Google can tighten or kill it silently.

"...only a problem if you have something to hide?"

Whistleblowers, journalists, and activists under authoritarian governments will be the first victims. People in domestic abuse situations are next. All these groups have legitimate reasons to distribute or use software without putting their legal identity in a Google database. Anonymous open-source contribution is a tradition older than Google itself. This policy ends it on Android.

"...the same thing Apple does?"

Apple has been a walled garden from day one. People chose Android because it was different. "Apple does it too" is a race to the bottom and a weak tu quoque argument. And under regulatory pressure (the EU's Digital Markets Act), even Apple is being forced to open up. Google is moving in the opposite direction: attempting to further entrench its gatekeeping status.

"...just $25 and some paperwork?"

Maybe, if you're a developer in the US with a credit card and a driver's license. Try being a student in sub-Saharan Africa, or a dissident in Myanmar, or a volunteer maintaining a community health app. The cost isn't only financial: you're surrendering government ID and evidence of your signing keys to a company that routinely complies with government demands to remove apps and expose developers.

Fight back

Everyone

  • Install F-Droid on every Android device you own. Alternative stores only survive if people actually use them.
  • Contact your regulators. Regulators worldwide are genuinely concerned about monopolies and the centralization of power in the tech sector, and want to hear directly from individuals who are affected and concerned.

item.title: Shitter – A Nitter Fork (147 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://codeberg.org/shitter/shitter, See on Hacker News

Shitter - a Nitter fork

A free and open source alternative Twitter front-end focused on privacy and performance.
Inspired by the Invidious project.

  • No JavaScript or ads
  • All requests go through the backend, client never talks to Twitter
  • Prevents Twitter from tracking your IP or JavaScript fingerprint
  • Uses Twitter's unofficial API (no developer account required)
  • Lightweight (thanks to @nim_lang, 60KB vs 784KB from twitter.com)
  • RSS feeds
  • Themes
  • Mobile support (responsive design)

Resources

The wiki contains:

  • List of public instances
  • Forks of the Nitter code repository
  • Browser extensions for auto-redirecting to Nitter
  • Guide: Self-hosting a Nitter instance
  • Guide: How to obtain session tokens
  • Guide: Using Nitter embeds

Contributing

This repository does not accept Pull Requests, but contributions are welcome in the form of Patch files, which can be submitted on an issue and are much more convenient to merge and work with.

Why?

It's impossible to use Twitter without JavaScript enabled, and as of 2024 you need to sign up. For privacy-minded folks, preventing JavaScript analytics and IP-based tracking is important, but apart from using a VPN and uBlock/uMatrix, it's impossible. Despite being behind a VPN and using heavy-duty adblockers, you can get accurately tracked with your browser's fingerprint, no JavaScript required. This all became particularly important after Twitter removed the ability for users to control whether their data gets sent to advertisers.

Using an instance of Nitter (hosted on a VPS for example), you can browse Twitter without JavaScript while retaining your privacy. In addition to respecting your privacy, Nitter is on average around 15 times lighter than Twitter, and in most cases serves pages faster (eg. timelines load 2-4x faster).

Screenshot

Install

Docker

Page for the Docker image: https://hub.docker.com/r/mv12star/shitter

NOTE: The published image is multi-arch — mv12star/shitter:latest runs natively on amd64/armv7/arm64.

To run Nitter with Docker, you'll need to install and run Redis separately before you can run the container. See below for how to also run Redis using Docker.

First create your config file. The Docker commands mount it into the container, so it has to exist on the host beforehand. If you've cloned the repo:

cp nitter.example.conf nitter.conf

If you're using the prebuilt image without a local clone, download nitter.example.conf and save it as nitter.conf instead.

To build and run Nitter in Docker:

docker build -t nitter:latest .
docker run -v $(pwd)/nitter.conf:/src/nitter.conf -d --network host nitter:latest

A prebuilt Docker image is provided as well:

docker run -v $(pwd)/nitter.conf:/src/nitter.conf -d --network host mv12star/shitter:latest

Using docker-compose to run both Nitter and Redis as different containers: Change redisHost from localhost to nitter-redis in nitter.conf, then run:

docker-compose up -d

Note the Docker commands mount nitter.conf (and sessions.jsonl for docker-compose) from the directory you run them in. If a mounted file doesn't exist, Docker silently creates a directory in its place and the container fails with not a directory: Are you trying to mount a directory onto a file. Remove that directory and create the file as shown above.

systemd

To run Nitter via systemd you can use this service file:

[Unit]
Description=Nitter (An alternative Twitter front-end)
After=syslog.target
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple

# set user and group
User=nitter
Group=nitter

# configure location
WorkingDirectory=/home/nitter/nitter
ExecStart=/home/nitter/nitter/nitter

Restart=always
RestartSec=15

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Then enable and run the service: systemctl enable --now nitter.service

Logging

Nitter currently prints some errors to stdout, and there is no real logging implemented. If you're running Nitter with systemd, you can check stdout like this: journalctl -u nitter.service (add --follow to see just the last 15 lines). If you're running the Docker image, you can do this: docker logs --follow *nitter container id*

Build from source

Dependencies

  • libpcre
  • libsass
  • redis/valkey

To compile Nitter you need a Nim installation, see nim-lang.org for details. It is possible to install it system-wide or in the user directory you create below.

To compile the scss files, you need to install libsass. On Ubuntu and Debian, you can use libsass-dev.

Redis is required for caching and in the future for account info. As of 2024 Redis is no longer open source, so using the fork Valkey is recommended. It should be available on most distros as redis or redis-server (Ubuntu/Debian), or valkey/valkey-server. Running it with the default config is fine, Nitter's default config is set to use the default port and localhost.

Here's how to create a nitter user, clone the repo, and build the project along with the scss and md files.

# useradd -m nitter
# su nitter
$ git clone https://codeberg.org/shitter/shitter
$ cd nitter
$ nimble -l build -d:danger --mm:refc
$ nimble -l scss
$ nimble -l md
$ cp nitter.example.conf nitter.conf

Set your hostname, port, HMAC key, https (must be correct for cookies), and Redis info in nitter.conf. To run Redis, either run redis-server --daemonize yes, or systemctl enable --now redis (or redis-server depending on the distro). Run Nitter by executing ./nitter or using the systemd service below. You should run Nitter behind a reverse proxy such as Nginx or Apache for security and performance reasons.

Matrix channel

Feel free to join our Matrix channel.

item.title: Hacker leaks 281 GB of data from Germany's far-right AfD party (153 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/hotforsecurity/hacker-leaks-281-gb-data-germany-afd, See on Hacker News

Germany's far-right AfD (Alternative für Deutschland) party has confirmed that it has suffered a security breach, after a hacker published what appear to be hundreds of thousands of the controversial political party's internal emails.

Earlier this week, the AfD admitted that its hosting provider had been hacked in September, and that some of its mailboxes had been copied. The party claims that most of the affected mailboxes had not been used for years, but the leaked archive reportedly includes messages dated as recently as 12 September 2026.

The news came as the Hexane.cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local media reports.

To add to the AfD's discomfort, reports suggest that the hacker's access may have been gained in an embarrassingly simple fashion, via a website that had allegedly been left unpatched. However, this has not been independently verified.

What is unusual is that the leaked emails are not published on the site directly. Instead, AI-generated summaries are shown, categorised and rated from Low to Critical. The site encourages anybody who wants to read a complete original email, including headers, message bodies, attachments, and DKIM signatures, to download it via a torrent.

Of course, everyone should be wary of trusting AI-generated summaries, as artificial intelligence has a history of making sometimes large mistakes with great confidence. Indeed, party sources told the media that although the leaked emails appeared to be authentic, the AI-generated summaries appeared to contain several inaccuracies.

The full corpus of 281 GB of stolen messages and files has been made available for download via the torrent, and claims to contain 421,179 stolen internal party emails as well as more than 100,000 files.

The hacker says the leak is intended to expose the party's "degeneracy and hypocrisy."

They have also claimed that someone with a Proton Mail email address reached out to them offering 100,000 Euros if the leak site was taken down.

Should you be tempted to download the torrent and explore the contents of the messages yourself? I would advise against it. In the past, cybercriminals have used torrents of trending topics in the public eye to distribute malware. That's before you even consider the possible legal questions that can arise from handling stolen personal data, whatever you might think of the individuals exposed.

It's not the first cybersecurity headache that the AfD has suffered recently. On 3 September, a press spokesman for the party's group in the Thuringia state parliament warned that his work email account had been used to send phishing emails, and urged recipients not to open PDF attachments they may have received.

Whatever you may think of the AfD, there appear to have been security failures in this case that are far too common. It's not unusual for websites to be overlooked or half-forgotten, and left unpatched. It's not rare for shared infrastructure to not be segmented properly.

Furthermore, whether you are an individual or an organisation, you should be aware that an email account can be a treasure trove of sensitive information. Even if it has not been used for years, it can hold vast amounts of correspondence that can be exploited by hackers and fraudsters.

URL: https://github.com/openssl/openssl/releases/tag/openssl-4.1.0, See on Hacker News

OpenSSL 4.1.0 is a feature release adding significant new functionality
to OpenSSL.

This release incorporates the following potentially significant or incompatible
changes:

  • Added VC-WIN32-MSVC2013 and VC-WIN64A-MSVC2013 build targets to provide
    internal functions for bridging the gaps in C99 standard support
    that are present in MSVC 2013.

  • Added optimized ML-DSA and ML-KEM NTT operations on ppc64le;
    optimized ML-DSA operations on x86_64;
    AVX-512-optimized SHAKE x4 operations for ML-DSA on x86_64;
    AVX-512 and VAES optimizations for AES-CBC decryption on x86_64.

  • Changed tsget utility to use Net::Curl::Easy (from the Net-Curl CPAN
    distribution) instead of the abandoned WWW::Curl::Easy. Users who rely
    on tsget should install Net::Curl::Easy before upgrading.

  • Dropped Windows-on-Itanium (VC-WIN64I) and Windows CE (VC-CE) targets
    from Configurations.

  • Dropped no-ecdsa and no-ecdh options from Configure, as these options
    did not really disable the implementations. Use no-ec to disable
    the elliptic curve support.

This release adds the following new features:

  • Support for DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147).
    Refer to the ossl-guide-dtlsv13(7) manual page for details.

  • Support for RFC 8701 GREASE (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain
    Extensibility).

  • DTLS support in the SSL listener API.

  • Support for IKEV2 KDF.

  • Initial support for the Elbrus2000 (e2k) architecture.

Known issues in 4.1.0:

  • #32878
    When a DTLS 1.3 KeyUpdate is received, all other outstanding
    post-handshake records are dropped from the retransmission buffer.
    This means post-handshake records still awaiting an ACK (such as a
    NewSessionTicket) will no longer be retransmitted if the original
    transmission is lost. A fix is in progress and planned for a future
    release.

  • #33277
    A permanent receive failure on a DTLS listener can be reported as
    SSL_ERROR_WANT_READ on an accepted connection. Polling and subsequent
    accept calls may also fail to report the error, causing applications
    to continue waiting after a permanent failure.

  • #33278
    A retryable write failure on a nonblocking connection accepted from a
    DTLS listener can be reported as SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL instead of
    SSL_ERROR_WANT_WRITE. Applications treating this result as fatal may
    close a connection that is still usable.

  • #33242
    DTLS 1.3 servers may abort handshakes with an unexpected_message alert
    when a client acknowledges part or all of the server's first flight
    before sending its response. This can occur after packet loss or while
    the client is preparing its authentication response.
